title: Spellman v. Commissioner
court: United States Court of Appeals, Seventh Circuit
subject: R&D Tax Shelter Partnerships and Section 174
summary: Spellman v. Commissioner, 845 F.2d 148 (7th Cir. 1988), holds that research expenditures are deductible under IRC § 174(a)(1) only if the taxpayer has a realistic prospect of exploiting the research in its own trade or business. For U.S. R&D investors and partnerships, passive financing of another company's research also fails the IRC § 41 R&D tax credit.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
Procedural Posture and Factual Background of the Claim

In Spellman v. Commissioner, 845 F.2d 148 (7th Cir. 1988), affirming the United States Tax Court's grant of summary judgment to the Commissioner, the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit addressed a foundational threshold question in federal research and development (R&D) taxation: under what circumstances do capital contributions and contract research payments made through a multi-tiered partnership satisfy the requirement of Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 174(a)(1) that research or experimental expenditures be paid or incurred "in connection with" the taxpayer's trade or business. Written by Circuit Judge Richard Posner on behalf of a panel that included Chief Judge Bauer and Senior Circuit Judge Pell, the appellate opinion stands as a seminal authority applying the economic substance and "realistic prospect" doctrines to R&D tax arrangements in the United States.

The dispute originated from federal income tax deficiencies assessed by the Commissioner of Internal Revenue against Burton L. and Roslyn Spellman following the disallowance of distributive partnership losses claimed as current research and experimental deductions under IRC § 174(a)(1). Burton and Roslyn Spellman were limited partners in Elmer South Oil Partnership, an investment partnership that, in turn, functioned as a limited partner in a second-tier limited partnership named Sci-Med, whose general partner was an Israeli company of which Teva was the parent. Under its partnership agreement, Sci-Med was organized to enter into a research and development agreement with Teva Pharmaceutical Industries (Teva), Israel's largest pharmaceutical manufacturer, for the purpose of developing new pharmaceutical compounds—specifically, novel penicillin antibiotics.

Pursuant to the R&D agreement, Sci-Med agreed to contribute $855,000—to be paid to Teva over time—to finance the research and development of the new penicillins. The contractual architecture between Sci-Med and Teva bifurcated the intellectual property rights into two categories: the primary research deliverables (the new penicillins) and secondary research deliverables ("byproducts," meaning antibiotics developed under the agreement but not as part of the specific project to develop new penicillins). With respect to the primary deliverables, the agreement granted Teva the exclusive rights to make, sell, and license the new penicillins, although the taxpayers contended that, as a matter of industry custom and therefore an implied term of the contract, these rights would not vest in Teva until the products were actually developed. In exchange for financing the research and granting Teva exclusive commercialization rights, Sci-Med was entitled to receive a royalty equal to 5 percent of Teva's revenues from the new penicillins until Sci-Med recovered its $855,000 contribution, after which the royalty rate dropped to 1 percent.

With respect to the secondary deliverables, the R&D agreement nominally reserved to Sci-Med the ownership rights to any byproducts developed outside the specific penicillin project. However, the agreement simultaneously gave Teva the right to purchase all of Sci-Med's rights to those byproducts for $20,000, and it separately granted Sci-Med the right to monitor Teva's research and development program in order to assure compliance with the agreement. On their federal income tax returns, the taxpayers claimed their allocable share of Sci-Med's $855,000 outlay—a largely future expenditure, because Sci-Med was to pay the $855,000 to Teva over time, which Elmer South sought to flow through at once to its cash-basis individual limited partners—as a current deduction under IRC § 174(a)(1), asserting that Sci-Med was engaged in, or had a realistic prospect of entering, the pharmaceutical trade or business.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) disallowed the claimed IRC § 174 deductions in full and moved for summary judgment in the United States Tax Court pursuant to Tax Court Rule 121. The Commissioner challenged the deductions on the ground that neither Sci-Med nor the upper-tier investment partnership was carrying on, or had any realistic probability of ever carrying on, a trade or business to which the pharmaceutical research expenditures could be connected.

In the view of the IRS, the transaction was an R&D tax shelter designed to convert nondeductible capital investments into immediate ordinary tax deductions for passive high-income investors. The Commissioner argued that Teva—not Sci-Med—was the sole entity conducting the pharmaceutical business, exercising control over the laboratory personnel, and possessing the manufacturing and marketing infrastructure required to commercialize the resulting compounds. Because Teva held exclusive commercialization rights to the primary penicillins in exchange for passive royalties and could acquire any valuable research byproducts for a nominal $20,000 payment, the Commissioner contended that Sci-Med functioned purely as a passive financial conduit.
Governing Statutory Framework in the United States

The statutory analysis in Spellman centers on the intersection of four core provisions of the Internal Revenue Code and their interpreting regulations and case law. As a foundational principle of U.S. tax law, expenditures that yield benefits extending beyond the current taxable year must generally be capitalized rather than deducted immediately. Under IRC § 162(a), ordinary and necessary expenses are deductible only if paid or incurred in "carrying on any trade or business," which requires that actual business operations have already commenced. Pre-opening or start-up expenses incurred prior to the commencement of an active going concern must be capitalized and amortized under IRC § 195.

Enacted in 1954 to encourage technological innovation and eliminate tax accounting uncertainty for early-stage enterprises, IRC § 174(a)(1) carved out an exception to the general capitalization rule by allowing taxpayers to deduct (or, for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021 and before January 1, 2025, and for foreign research thereafter, amortize over prescribed statutory periods, with immediate expensing of domestic research expenditures restored under new IRC § 174A, enacted by Public Law 119-21 on July 4, 2025, for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024) "research or experimental expenditures which are paid or incurred by him during the taxable year in connection with his trade or business". Under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a), qualifying expenditures must represent research and development costs in the "experimental or laboratory sense" aimed at eliminating uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product, and under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(2), they include amounts paid to another person or organization for research performed "on behalf of" the taxpayer. Furthermore, IRC § 174(e) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(6) restrict eligibility to expenditures that are "reasonable under the circumstances".

In Snow v. Commissioner, 416 U.S. 500 (1974), the U.S. Supreme Court contrasted the narrow "carrying on" language of IRC § 162(a) with the broader "in connection with" phrasing of IRC § 174(a)(1), holding that a start-up enterprise need not currently be producing or selling goods to deduct R&D expenditures. However, as Judge Posner observed in Spellman, the Supreme Court's broad reading of § 174(a)(1) in Snow "fairly invited the creation of R&D tax shelters, and the bar quickly took up the invitation". To prevent passive investors from claiming § 174 deductions for financing another corporation's business, the Tax Court in Green v. Commissioner, 83 T.C. 667 (1984), and the federal appellate courts established that Snow relaxed only the temporal nexus to a trade or business, not the operational nexus. The taxpayer must still establish that it will engage in a trade or business of its own at some point, rather than merely functioning as a passive investor collecting royalties or dividends.

While Spellman litigated the underlying deduction under IRC § 174(a)(1), its holding directly governs eligibility for the federal Research and Development Tax Credit under IRC § 41. Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A)—the first prong of the mandatory Four-Part Test for "qualified research"—an activity cannot constitute qualified research unless the expenditures with respect to such activity "may be treated as expenses under section 174". As confirmed in Norwest Corp. v. Commissioner, 110 T.C. 454, 491 (1998) and IRS Chief Counsel advisories, a taxpayer cannot circumvent the restrictions of § 174 when claiming Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) under § 41(b); failure to satisfy all elements of § 174, including the "in connection with a trade or business" requirement as interpreted by Spellman, results in complete disqualification of the claimed R&D tax credit. Moreover, for purposes of § 41, the taxpayer must satisfy the even stricter trade or business standard of § 41(b)(1) ("in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer"), the contract research rules of § 41(b)(3) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e), and the funded research and substantial rights exclusions under § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d).
The Court's Final Holding

The Seventh Circuit unanimously affirmed the Tax Court's entry of summary judgment in favor of the Commissioner. Articulating the governing legal test, Judge Posner held that Snow makes it important to determine whether the prospects for developing a new product that will be exploited in a business of the taxpayer are realistic, and that if those prospects are not realistic, the research expenditure cannot be "in connection with" a business of the taxpayer under IRC § 174(a)(1).

Evaluating the economic substance of the Sci-Med/Teva agreements, the court concluded that no such realistic prospect existed. With respect to the primary penicillin compounds, Sci-Med had dealt away to Teva the exclusive rights to make and sell the new penicillins in exchange for a royalty stream, and the court held that even if, as the taxpayers argued, those rights would not vest in Teva until the products were developed, that reservation would no more put Sci-Med in the pharmaceutical business than foreclosing on a real estate mortgage would make a bank a real estate company; likewise, Sci-Med's right to monitor Teva's program no more made it a pharmaceutical business than a debenture trustee's right to inspect an issuer's books and plants would make bondholders joint venturers with the issuing corporation. With respect to the research byproducts, Teva's option to purchase all byproduct rights for a mere $20,000 created an insurmountable economic barrier: if the byproducts proved commercially valuable (worth more than $20,000), Teva was certain to exercise the option, leaving Sci-Med with nothing to exploit. Conversely, if the byproducts proved to be worth less than $20,000, Sci-Med would retain the right to market them but would not exercise it, because exploiting rights worth at most $20,000 would require Sci-Med to acquire staff, facilities, and pharmaceutical expertise from the ground up at a cost exceeding any possible profit, and Sci-Med presented no evidence that it had, or was likely ever to acquire, a staff, relevant experience, or anything else indicating a likelihood or intention of entering the business. Consequently, the court found the prospect of Sci-Med entering a trade or business under IRC § 174(a)(1) to be "remote," so clearly so that a trial was not required, and the Tax Court properly granted summary judgment under Tax Court Rule 121 without holding an evidentiary trial.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

The disqualification of the R&D claim in Spellman v. Commissioner resulted from a convergence of structural contract flaws, operational deficiencies, and procedural evidentiary failures. For tax practitioners and technical advisors evaluating modern R&D claims under IRC §§ 174 and 41, dissecting these specific failures reveals how courts scrutinize the economic reality of outsourced R&D, joint ventures, and technology licensing arrangements.
Failure to Establish a "Realistic Prospect" of Entering a Trade or Business

The primary legal deficiency in Spellman was the partnership's inability to bridge the gap between passive capital investment and active business operations. Taxpayers frequently misinterpret Snow v. Commissioner, 416 U.S. 500 (1974), as granting carte blanche to deduct R&D expenditures whenever an entity funds technological development. In Spellman, the Seventh Circuit clarified that Snow merely eliminated the requirement that a taxpayer already be selling products during the year the research is conducted; it did not eliminate the statutory requirement that the research be conducted for the taxpayer's own prospective trade or business.

Under the line of authority applying the Spellman realistic-prospect inquiry—including cases such as Kantor v. Commissioner, 998 F.2d 1514 (9th Cir. 1993), Diamond v. Commissioner, 930 F.2d 372 (4th Cir. 1991), and Harris v. Commissioner, 16 F.3d 75 (5th Cir. 1994)—courts have framed the test as requiring a taxpayer to demonstrate two cumulative elements at the time the research expenditures are incurred, although Spellman itself did not articulate a formal two-part test. First, the taxpayer must manifest an objective intent, meaning a bona fide, demonstrable business purpose and operational plan to manufacture, market, or actively exploit the developed technology in a going concern, rather than merely licensing it away passively or selling it for capital gain. Second, the taxpayer must possess operational capability, defined as the practical financial, technical, managerial, and infrastructural capacity to actually execute that business plan.

Courts applying this inquiry have observed that "in the abstract everybody has the 'capacity' to engage in a trade or business," so the legal inquiry turns on probability rather than mere possibility; Spellman itself, following the Seventh Circuit's earlier decision in Levin v. Commissioner, 832 F.2d 403 (7th Cir. 1987) (see also Goulding v. Commissioner, 928 F.2d 1135 (7th Cir. 1991)), framed the question as whether the prospects were realistic and found Sci-Med's prospect "remote". Sci-Med failed both prongs. Sci-Med presented no evidence that it had, or was likely ever to acquire, a staff, relevant experience, or anything else indicating a likelihood or intention of entering the pharmaceutical business, and its $855,000 commitment was to be paid to Teva over time to fund Teva's research. Because entering the pharmaceutical manufacturing or marketing sector requires massive capital outlays and specialized regulatory apparatus, Sci-Med lacked the objective capability to exploit any resulting drug candidates on its own.
The Contractual Buyout Option Trap and Asymmetric Economic Reality

The fatal contractual flaw in Spellman—and the centerpiece of Judge Posner's economic analysis—was the combination of an exclusive grant to Teva of the rights to make and sell the primary technology with a nominal fixed-price purchase option ($20,000) covering the research byproducts. Tax shelter promoters and poorly advised joint ventures frequently insert residual ownership clauses (such as retaining rights to "byproducts" or allowing the funding entity to commercialize the technology if the research contractor declines an option) to create the illusion on paper that the funding entity might someday operate a business.

Although the opinion does not cite Gregory v. Helvering, 293 U.S. 465 (1935), the Seventh Circuit, in a manner consistent with the substance-over-form doctrine originating in that case, looked past the formal recitals of the contract to evaluate the economic incentives governing the parties' behavior across all plausible outcomes. Under a successful research scenario yielding high-value byproducts whose expected net present value exceeded $20,000, Teva—as a rational economic actor already in possession of the laboratory data and manufacturing facilities—was virtually guaranteed to exercise its $20,000 call option. Upon exercise, Sci-Med's rights to the byproducts would be extinguished prior to any commercial exploitation. Conversely, under an unsuccessful or low-value research scenario where Teva elected not to exercise the $20,000 option, that decision would reflect the assessment of an established pharmaceutical manufacturer that the byproducts were worth less than $20,000. The court also considered the possibility that the byproducts might be worth more than $20,000 yet Teva might mistakenly fail to exercise its option, but deemed that eventuality unlikely because Teva rather than Sci-Med was the pharmaceutical company, and in any event it would not pay Sci-Med to exploit rights worth at most $20,000 when doing so would require acquiring staff, facilities, and pharmaceutical expertise from the ground up—an economically irrational undertaking.

Thus, under every plausible economic outcome, the contractual option structure ensured that Sci-Med would never actively commercialize the research results. In economic substance, the $855,000 payment was not an operational R&D expenditure of Sci-Med's business but, as the court explained, akin to a nondeductible capital contribution financing Teva's R&D in exchange for royalties—equivalent to the purchase price of a share in an oil lease—with a return consisting of the 5 percent royalty (dropping to 1 percent after recoupment of the $855,000) plus a potential $20,000 option payout.
Passive Investor Status and Complete Delegation of Technical Control

Closely tied to the contractual option trap was Sci-Med's lack of any operational involvement in the research program beyond a contractual right to monitor. Under the R&D agreement, Teva—not Sci-Med—performed the research and development, while Sci-Med's role was limited to a right to monitor Teva's research and development program in order to assure compliance with the agreement. Sci-Med presented no evidence that it employed scientists or had relevant experience, and the court held that its monitoring right no more put it into the pharmaceutical business than a bond debenture entitling the debenture trustee to inspect the issuer's books and plants would make the bondholders joint venturers with the issuing corporation (citing Whipple v. Commissioner, 373 U.S. 193 (1963), and Green v. Commissioner, 83 T.C. at 690).

Courts consistently hold that where a taxpayer delegates complete technical and operational authority to an independent research contractor and retains neither active supervisory control nor the operational infrastructure to use the research results, the taxpayer's activities do not rise to the level of a trade or business. While Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(2) permits a taxpayer to deduct costs paid to a contractor for research performed "on behalf of" the taxpayer, that regulation presupposes that the hiring taxpayer is itself engaged in (or realistically entering) an active trade or business that will utilize the research output. Paying a third party to conduct research that the third party will exclusively manufacture and sell may cause the payer to be viewed as an investor rather than an entrepreneur—a point the Seventh Circuit noted but expressly declined to decide—and the court held that a payer merely financing the contractor's research in exchange for royalties makes a nondeductible capital contribution rather than a deductible expense.
Intersection with Modern IRC § 41 R&D Tax Credit Disqualification Mechanics

When the factual and contractual deficiencies identified in Spellman occur in a contemporary R&D tax credit claim under IRC § 41, they trigger cascading disqualifications across four distinct statutory and regulatory provisions. First, the claim fails the IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) Section 174 eligibility prong. To qualify for the research credit under IRC § 41(a)(1), the activity must first constitute "qualified research" under § 41(d)(1), which mandates at subparagraph (A) that associated expenditures "may be treated as expenses under section 174". Because a Spellman failure means the expenditures are not incurred "in connection with" the taxpayer's trade or business under § 174(a)(1), the entire project fails the first prong of the Four-Part Test ab initio.

Second, the arrangement fails the IRC § 41(b)(1) "carrying on" standard. Even if a pre-operational venture satisfied the relaxed "in connection with" standard of § 174(a)(1) under Snow and Spellman, IRC § 41(b)(1) imposes a stricter threshold for QREs: expenses must be paid or incurred by the taxpayer "in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer" (mirroring the active business standard of IRC § 162), unless the taxpayer qualifies under the narrow start-up rules for in-house research expenses under § 41(b)(4). Passive investment partnerships and special-purpose financing vehicles fail § 41(b)(1) outright.

Third, the structure runs afoul of the contract research rules under IRC § 41(b)(3) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e) as well as the funded research exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d). Section 41 enforces a "mirror rule" governing outsourced R&D to ensure that both the payer and the researcher do not claim the credit for the same expenditures. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(1)-(3), a payer may claim 65 percent of amounts paid to a contractor as "contract research expenses" only if the research is performed on behalf of the taxpayer, meaning the taxpayer must enter into the agreement prior to performance of the research, bear the financial risk of failure by requiring payment regardless of success, and have a right to the research results. Conversely, under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), a researcher performing work for another party is barred from claiming the credit ("funded research") unless the researcher retains substantial rights in the research and bears the financial risk because payment is contingent on success. Crucially, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3) provides that a taxpayer does not retain substantial rights in the research if the taxpayer must pay for the right to use the results of the research. In a Spellman arrangement, the funding entity (Sci-Med) fails because it has pre-assigned exclusive rights to the primary research to the contractor and stripped itself of substantial operational rights via the nominal $20,000 call option, while the contractor (Teva) faces a "substantial rights" and "funded research" challenge under § 41(d)(4)(H) if its capital was reimbursed on a non-contingent basis or if it must pay a royalty or option exercise price to acquire the byproduct rights. As tax commentators and courts have noted, poorly structured two-party R&D contracts can result in a "whipsaw" where neither party qualifies for the § 41 credit.

Fourth, such arrangements routinely fail the requirements for substantiation of technological uncertainty, process of experimentation, and reasonable compensation under IRC §§ 41(d)(1)(B)-(C) and 174(e). Beyond the contractual and trade-or-business defects, taxpayers in Spellman-type disputes routinely lack contemporaneous technical documentation proving that the underlying expenditures were incurred in the "experimental or laboratory sense" to eliminate scientific or technological uncertainty (Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1); Coors Porcelain Co. v. Commissioner, 52 T.C. 682 (1969), aff'd, 429 F.2d 1 (10th Cir. 1970)) or that substantially all activities constituted elements of a structured process of experimentation (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C); Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner; Agro Science Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1989-687, aff'd, 934 F.2d 573 (5th Cir. 1991)). Furthermore, when R&D partnerships inflate upfront contract payments or executive compensation using promissory notes or circular financing, the IRS invokes IRC § 174(e) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(6) to disallow any portion of the expenditure that exceeds a "reasonable" amount for the research services actually performed.
Procedural and Evidentiary Failure at Summary Judgment

A critical procedural legacy of Spellman v. Commissioner is its rigorous application of summary judgment standards to tax litigation. On appeal, the taxpayers argued that the case was "overflowing" with factual issues—including whether Sci-Med intended or had the prospect to enter a trade or business with the research byproducts—that could not be resolved on summary judgment under Tax Court Rule 121 without a trial.

Judge Posner flatly rejected this argument, establishing a procedural standard cited extensively across federal jurisprudence. The court noted that the pertinent language of Tax Court Rule 121(b) ("that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and that a decision may be rendered as a matter of law") is materially identical to that of Rule 56(c) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. Relying on Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)—one of the U.S. Supreme Court's 1986 summary judgment trilogy alongside Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986), and Matsushita Electric Industrial Co. v. Zenith Radio Corp., 475 U.S. 574 (1986), which the opinion does not cite—and on Barker v. Henderson, Franklin, Starnes & Holt, 797 F.2d 490 (7th Cir. 1986), the Seventh Circuit held that the question is whether the factual issues, if resolved in the taxpayers' favor, would show entitlement to the deduction, and that if, when discovery is completed, the party with the burden of proof has failed to obtain enough evidence to defeat a motion for directed verdict, its opponent is entitled to summary judgment.

Specifically, Spellman established that issues of motive, business purpose, or prospective intent do not immunize a taxpayer from summary judgment when the objective economic terms of the governing contracts render the taxpayer's claimed intent implausible. Under Rule 56(e) and Tax Court Rule 121, a taxpayer opposing summary judgment cannot rely on conclusory affidavits, uncorroborated assertions of possible future business operations, or inadmissible hearsay. When the written R&D and licensing agreements leave only a speculative possibility—rather than a realistic probability—that the taxpayer will ever commercialize the research in its own business, the court must grant summary judgment to the IRS as a matter of law without holding an evidentiary hearing.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory, regulatory, and procedural requirement implicated in Spellman v. Commissioner (and its modern IRC § 41 counterparts) against the specific deficiencies of the taxpayer's claim and the governing standard of proof applied by United States federal courts.

headers: Court's Standard of Proof & Evidentiary Threshold

cells: Trade or Business Nexus ("In Connection With")
IRC § 174(a)(1); Snow v. Commissioner, 416 U.S. 500 (1974); Green v. Commissioner, 83 T.C. 667 (1984); Spellman v. Commissioner, 845 F.2d 148 (7th Cir. 1988).
Sci-Med acted solely as a passive investment vehicle channeling $855,000 to Teva; it never commenced business operations and had no operational nexus to pharmaceutical manufacturing or marketing.

Realistic Prospect Standard: The taxpayer must prove by objective evidence both (1) a bona fide objective intent to enter a trade or business of its own, and (2) the practical capability (financial, technical, infrastructural) to do so. Probability, not mere possibility, is required.
Commercialization Rights to Primary Research Output
IRC § 174(a)(1); Levin v. Commissioner, 832 F.2d 403 (7th Cir. 1987); Harris v. Commissioner, 16 F.3d 75 (5th Cir. 1994).

Sci-Med granted Teva the exclusive rights to make, sell, and license the primary deliverables (new penicillins) in exchange for a passive 5% revenue royalty until recoupment of the $855,000 investment and a 1% royalty thereafter.

Active Exploitation vs. Passive Royalty Test: Financing another entity's research in exchange for passive royalties, dividends, or capital appreciation constitutes an investment in the business of another, not a trade or business of the taxpayer.
Economic Substance of Residual / Byproduct Options
IRC § 174(a)(1); Gregory v. Helvering, 293 U.S. 465 (1935); Spellman, 845 F.2d at 150–51; Diamond v. Commissioner, 930 F.2d 372 (4th Cir. 1991); Kantor v. Commissioner, 998 F.2d 1514 (9th Cir. 1993).

Although Sci-Med nominally retained rights to research "byproducts," Teva held the right to buy all of Sci-Med's byproduct rights for a nominal $20,000—ensuring Teva would buy any byproducts worth more than $20,000 and leave Sci-Med only with rights it would not economically exploit.

Economic Reality / Substance-Over-Form Test: Courts evaluate the economic incentives at contract execution. A below-market or nominal buyout option eliminates any realistic prospect of the grantor exploiting the technology, rendering residual ownership illusory.
Operational Control & Supervision of Contract Research
Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(2); Kantor, 998 F.2d at 1519; LDL Research & Dev. II, Ltd. v. Commissioner, 124 F.3d 1338 (10th Cir. 1997); I-Tech R&D Ltd. Partnership v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2001-103.

Teva performed the R&D program, while Sci-Med retained only a contractual right to monitor Teva's research and development program to assure compliance with the agreement—a right the court held did not put Sci-Med into the pharmaceutical business.

Active Involvement & Direction Standard: While research may be contracted out under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(2), the payer must maintain active business governance, technical oversight, or operational capability to integrate the results into its own business.
Section 41 R&D Credit Gateway & Trade or Business Threshold
IRC § 41(a)(1), § 41(b)(1), § 41(d)(1)(A); Norwest Corp. v. Commissioner, 110 T.C. 454 (1998); Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50.

Disqualification under IRC § 174(a)(1) automatically causes total failure of the IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) gateway test; passive partnership structure also fails the stricter "carrying on" requirement of IRC § 41(b)(1).

Strict Statutory Compliance: The taxpayer bears the burden of proving that all claimed QREs satisfy every element of IRC § 174 deductibility/amortization plus the active "carrying on" standard of IRC § 41(b)(1).
Substantial Rights & Unfunded Research Status

Sci-Med stripped itself of substantial rights by pre-licensing the penicillins exclusively to Teva and granting the $20,000 byproduct call option; conversely, requiring payment to use research results destroys substantial rights.

Substantial Rights & Financial Risk Mirror Rules: The claimant must prove through the four corners of the contract that it retains substantial rights to use the research results without paying additional consideration and bears the financial risk of technical failure.
Experimental Sense, Process of Experimentation & Reasonable Cost
IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)–(C), § 174(e); Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), (6); Coors Porcelain Co. v. Commissioner, 52 T.C. 682 (1969); Agro Science Co. v. Commissioner, 934 F.2d 573 (5th Cir. 1991).

The Spellman court did not reach these issues; in a comparable arrangement, the absence of taxpayer-level technical records demonstrating scientific uncertainty, hypothesis testing, or reasonable valuation of the $855,000 outlay (payable to Teva over time) relative to specific experimental tasks would present an additional vulnerability.

Contemporaneous Technical & Financial Substantiation: The taxpayer must produce contemporaneous laboratory/engineering records proving scientific experimentation aimed at resolving technological uncertainty and demonstrable reasonableness of costs under IRC § 174(e).
Procedural Summary Judgment Opposition
Tax Court Rule 121; Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(c), (e); Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986); Spellman, 845 F.2d at 151–52.

The taxpayers argued the case was "overflowing" with factual issues, including whether Sci-Med might develop the byproducts if Teva declined the $20,000 option, but Sci-Med presented no evidence that it had or was likely to acquire staff, relevant experience, or anything else indicating probable business entry.

Specific Admissible Facts & Outcome-Determinative Standard: Non-movant must submit admissible, non-conclusory evidence demonstrating a genuine issue of material fact; theoretical possibilities contradicted by contractual economics fail as a matter of law.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the holdings of Spellman v. Commissioner and related U.S. federal jurisprudence into actionable compliance protocols, the following two applied industry case studies examine realistic corporate R&D initiatives that initially suffer from the exact legal, contractual, and evidentiary defects identified by the Seventh Circuit. Each case study provides a rigorous, step-by-step restructuring plan across project governance, technical documentation, contract drafting, and experimentation tracking to secure full eligibility under IRC §§ 174 and 41.
Case Study 1: Biopharmaceutical Joint Venture & Outsourced Drug Discovery
Initial Defective Fact Pattern

BioVanguard Holdings LLC ("BioVanguard"), a newly formed Delaware limited liability company taxed as a partnership, raises $4.5 million from accredited investors to develop novel small-molecule beta-lactamase inhibitors designed to restore the efficacy of beta-lactam antibiotics against multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria. Having no wet-lab facilities or full-time scientific staff, BioVanguard enters into a Master Development and Commercialization Agreement (MDCA) with PharmaCore Inc. ("PharmaCore"), an established contract development and manufacturing organization (CDMO) with proprietary high-throughput screening facilities.

Under the initial MDCA, BioVanguard transfers $4.2 million upfront to PharmaCore to conduct lead optimization, in vitro minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) assays, and murine pharmacokinetic and toxicology studies. The MDCA contains three fatal Spellman defects. First, PharmaCore is granted an immediate, worldwide exclusive license to manufacture, gain FDA approval for, and commercialize all resulting beta-lactamase inhibitors in exchange for paying BioVanguard a 4 percent royalty on net commercial sales until BioVanguard recovers $4.2 million, and 1.5 percent thereafter. Second, BioVanguard nominally retains title to "Secondary Assay Byproducts" (chemical scaffolds showing activity against non-bacterial targets such as fungal or oncology pathways), but grants PharmaCore an exclusive 36-month option to purchase all rights to any Secondary Assay Byproducts for a flat fee of $50,000. Third, Section 14 of the MDCA states that PharmaCore is an independent contractor maintaining sole and exclusive control over all research personnel, experimental design, and regulatory filings, while BioVanguard receives only quarterly financial summary invoices.

If audited by the IRS, BioVanguard's claimed IRC § 174 amortization or deductions and IRC § 41 contract research tax credits (65 percent of $4.2 million, or $2.73 million in claimed QREs) will be disallowed on summary judgment under Spellman, Kantor, and Diamond. BioVanguard has no realistic prospect of entering a pharmaceutical trade or business because PharmaCore holds exclusive rights to the primary drugs, PharmaCore will inevitably exercise the $50,000 option on any commercially viable byproducts, and BioVanguard lacks the capital ($300,000 remaining reserve) and technical personnel to commercialize unexercised marginal byproducts.
Step 1: Restructuring Corporate and Project Governance to Establish Operational Capability and Nexus

To satisfy the Spellman "realistic prospect" test (both objective intent and capability) and the active business nexus of IRC §§ 174(a)(1) and 41(b)(1), BioVanguard must transform itself from a passive investment syndicate into an active operational biotechnology enterprise prior to incurring R&D expenses. BioVanguard must hire or retain at least two qualified internal officers—a Chief Scientific Officer (holding a Ph.D. in medicinal chemistry) and a Vice President of Regulatory and Clinical Affairs—on W-2 payroll. Furthermore, the MDCA must establish a Joint Technical Steering Committee (JSC) chaired by BioVanguard's CSO, holding final decision-making authority over target product profiles, chemical synthesis pathways, go/no-go stage gates, and assay protocols.

Rather than disbursing 93 percent of raised capital ($4.2 million of $4.5 million) in a single upfront transfer that leaves the entity unable to fund follow-on commercialization, BioVanguard must structure staged milestone funding (such as $1.8 million for Phase I lead optimization) while retaining $2.7 million in committed working capital and documented credit or venture facilities earmarked for Investigational New Drug (IND) enabling studies, third-party cGMP contract manufacturing, and specialty hospital distribution. Finally, BioVanguard—not PharmaCore—must be designated as the sole holder and sponsor of all Pre-IND and IND applications filed with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), directly curing the regulatory authority defect highlighted in IRS Field Service Advice 200145011.
Step 2: Re-Engineering Contractual Terms, Option Pricing, and Substantial Rights

To eliminate the Spellman option trap and satisfy the contract research and substantial rights rules of IRC §§ 41(b)(3), 41(d)(4)(H), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e), and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), the parties must execute a comprehensive Amended and Restated Master Services Agreement (MSA) prior to the performance of any qualified research. The parties must rescind the upfront exclusive commercialization license to PharmaCore so that BioVanguard retains 100 percent ownership of all intellectual property, patents, chemical entities, and assay data generated under the program ("Foreground IP"), covering both the primary beta-lactamase inhibitors and all secondary byproducts.

Simultaneously, the fixed $50,000 call option on research byproducts must be eliminated. If PharmaCore desires an avenue to license resulting compounds, BioVanguard may grant PharmaCore only a time-limited Right of First Negotiation (ROFN) exercisable after proof-of-concept completion, under which any license or acquisition price must be negotiated at arm's length based on an independent third-party valuation of Fair Market Value (FMV) at the time of exercise, or structure a co-promotion joint venture where BioVanguard actively manufactures or co-markets the product in North America while licensing ex-U.S. territories. Even under IRS scrutiny of significant exercise prices, an unpriced ROFN or FMV appraisal mechanism after technical completion prevents the automatic stripping of valuable IP that doomed Spellman. To comply with Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e) financial risk allocation rules, PharmaCore's compensation must be structured on a time-and-materials or stage-gated fee-for-service basis where BioVanguard is contractually obligated to pay for the research stages performed regardless of whether the compounds succeed technically. The MSA must explicitly stipulate that PharmaCore performs the research "on behalf of" BioVanguard, that BioVanguard bears the full financial risk of experimental failure, and that BioVanguard retains exclusive substantial rights to use and commercialize the research results without paying any royalty or option fee to PharmaCore.
Step 3: Technical Documentation of Scientific Uncertainty and Process of Experimentation

To satisfy Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1) ("experimental or laboratory sense") and the Four-Part Test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(A)–(D), BioVanguard's CSO and PharmaCore's lead chemists must establish a structured technical documentation protocol. Prior to each synthesis cycle, the scientific team must document the exact baseline technological uncertainty—specifically, why existing beta-lactamase inhibitor scaffolds fail to penetrate the outer membrane porins of Pseudomonas aeruginosa without inducing dose-limiting nephrotoxicity, establishing that the optimal molecular configuration cannot be known or determined from publicly available scientific literature.

Throughout execution, the team must record a hypothesis-driven process of experimentation capturing the formulation of specific biochemical hypotheses (such as substituting polar zwitterionic side chains at the C-3 position to enhance porin permeation), the systematic computational modeling via molecular docking simulations, the synthesis of 45 structural analogs, and the comparative in vitro MIC and cytotoxicity testing against control strains. Every experimental assay must be mapped directly to a defined Business Component under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B)—specifically, the candidate drug formulation (Compound Series BV-204)—demonstrating that the research aims to achieve a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality under IRC § 41(d)(3)(A).
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking, Cost Accounting, and Summary Judgment Readiness

To survive IRS examination and prevent an adverse summary judgment motion under Tax Court Rule 121 and Fed. R. Civ. P. 56, BioVanguard must implement contemporaneous financial and evidentiary controls. Lump-sum upfront invoices must be prohibited in favor of monthly itemized invoices from PharmaCore breaking down hours by scientist, hourly billing rates benchmarked to industry CDMO norms (satisfying IRC § 174(e) reasonableness), consumable laboratory supplies, and specific experimental work-package codes, while explicitly excluding any patent litigation, market research, or administrative overhead.

Concurrently, BioVanguard's CSO and VP of Regulatory Affairs must maintain weekly contemporaneous time logs tracking hours spent directly supervising PharmaCore's chemists, reviewing mass spectrometry and assay datasets, and directing structural modifications under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c). By compiling an indexed Rule 56 and Rule 121 audit defense file containing JSC meeting minutes, signed IND regulatory submissions, third-party cGMP manufacturing term sheets, and commercialization financial models, BioVanguard will possess concrete, admissible facts proving active business governance and commercial capability, defeating any IRS motion for summary judgment.
Case Study 2: Semiconductor & Photonic Hardware Spin-Out Syndicate
Initial Defective Fact Pattern

OptiCore Ventures LP ("OptiCore") is organized by a group of technology executives and venture investors to fund the development of a next-generation silicon-photonic optical interconnect chip ("OptiLink-X") capable of 1.6 Terabits-per-second (Tbps) data transmission for hyperscale AI data centers. OptiCore is formed in the same office suite as SiliconWave Foundry Corp. ("SiliconWave"), an established semiconductor manufacturer whose corporate officers also serve as the managing directors of OptiCore's general partner.

OptiCore raises $6.0 million and immediately enters into three interlocking agreements with SiliconWave: a Technology License Agreement, a Research and Development Agreement, and a Purchase Option Agreement. First, operating as a captive conduit structure, OptiCore has no cleanroom facilities, no Electronic Design Automation (EDA) software licenses, no hardware engineers, and no sales force, and it pays $5.8 million to SiliconWave to design, fabricate, and test prototype photonic wafers. Second, under the agreements, SiliconWave is appointed as OptiCore's exclusive agent to manufacture and sell the resulting photonic chips, and if OptiCore fails to raise additional capital or breaches any obligation, all technology rights revert automatically to SiliconWave. Third, under the Purchase Option Agreement, SiliconWave holds an irrevocable option to acquire either 100 percent of the developed OptiLink-X IP or all outstanding partnership units of OptiCore in exchange for a fixed payment of $150,000 in cash or SiliconWave common stock. Meanwhile, SiliconWave also attempts to claim in-house R&D tax credits under IRC § 41(b)(2) for the engineering wages of its foundry staff working on the OptiLink-X project.

Under Spellman v. Commissioner, Levin v. Commissioner, and IRS Field Service Advice 200145011, this arrangement creates a catastrophic double tax failure. OptiCore's § 174 deductions and § 41 contract research credits are disallowed in full because OptiCore is merely a financing device designed to pump capital into SiliconWave; the interlocking management, lack of independent facilities, and $150,000 call option prove that OptiCore has no realistic prospect of independently manufacturing or marketing photonic semiconductors. At the same time, SiliconWave's claimed in-house § 41 credits are disallowed under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) because its research was fully funded by OptiCore's non-contingent $5.8 million payment, and SiliconWave must pay $150,000 (or royalties) to acquire the right to use the research results, violating Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3) ("A taxpayer does not retain substantial rights in the research if the taxpayer must pay for the right to use the results of the research"). Consequently, neither entity receives the R&D tax credit.
Step 1: Restructuring Corporate Independence and Operational Governance

To establish that the taxpayer claiming the IRC §§ 174 and 41 tax benefits is engaged in its own active trade or business rather than financing the business of another, the parties must eliminate the hybrid tax-shelter architecture and adopt a bona fide operational fabless semiconductor model. OptiCore must be converted into an active operating corporation or LLC ("OptiCore Semiconductor Inc.") with independent corporate governance, separate physical office and optical testing lab space, and an independent board of directors not controlled by SiliconWave officers.

Crucially, OptiCore must directly employ its own core integrated-circuit (IC) architecture team—including Principal Photonic Architects, RTL/VLSI Design Engineers, and Thermal Packaging Engineers—using licensed EDA simulation tools in-house. SiliconWave's role must be strictly confined to that of a third-party semiconductor wafer foundry executing multi-project wafer (MPW) fabrication runs according to GDSII layout files designed and owned by OptiCore. Furthermore, OptiCore must retain at least 40 percent of its raised capital internally to fund internal engineering salaries, optical test benches, and direct OEM sales engineering targeting hyperscale cloud providers, establishing an undeniable probability and active commencement of going concern operations under IRC §§ 162, 174, and 41(b)(1).
Step 2: Re-Engineering Contractual Risk, IP Ownership, and the Funded Research Mirror Rules

To prevent the "nobody gets the credit" whipsaw under IRC § 41(b)(3) and § 41(d)(4)(H), the contracts between OptiCore and SiliconWave must cleanly allocate substantial rights and financial risk. The parties must terminate the Purchase Option Agreement and Exclusive Manufacturing and Marketing Agency Agreement in their entirety so that SiliconWave holds no option—nominal or otherwise—to buy out OptiCore's equity or acquire the OptiLink-X chip designs.

To enable OptiCore to claim the QREs (consisting of 100 percent of its in-house engineering wages and supplies plus 65 percent of its contract research payments to SiliconWave), the Foundry Services Agreement must vest 100 percent of all mask sets, GDSII chip layouts, and photonic waveguide IP exclusively in OptiCore without any payment required to use the results. OptiCore must pay SiliconWave per-wafer fabrication fees contingent on SiliconWave following OptiCore's design specifications rather than contingent on whether OptiCore's photonic circuit architecture achieves the 1.6 Tbps target performance, thereby placing the technical and financial risk of R&D failure squarely on OptiCore. Conversely, if SiliconWave performs distinct internal process R&D to modify its own foundry lithography tooling, the parties should separate that scope into an independent contract where SiliconWave bears the financial risk—with payment contingent on delivering certified prototype wafers passing strict quality assurance, bit-error-rate acceptance tests, and inspection barometers—and retains substantial rights to use the fabrication process technology across all foundry customers without paying OptiCore. This clean contractual bifurcation allows OptiCore to claim credits on its chip architecture QREs while SiliconWave claims credits on its unfunded foundry process QREs without statutory overlap.
Step 3: Technical Documentation of Photonic Engineering Uncertainties and Iterative Experimentation

To substantiate that the expenditures qualify as experimental laboratory research under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a) and meet the Four-Part Test of IRC § 41(d)(1), OptiCore must institute rigorous engineering documentation standards. The engineering team must formally document why achieving 1.6 Tbps optical modulation across silicon-nitride waveguides within a 15-watt thermal envelope presents fundamental capability and design uncertainties under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1)—specifically, overcoming nonlinear two-photon absorption (TPA), free-carrier dispersion losses, and thermal crosstalk between adjacent Mach-Zehnder modulator channels.

To prove a structured process of experimentation under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), OptiCore must maintain version-controlled Git and EDA repositories capturing the systematic evaluation of design alternatives. These technical records must trace the progression from formulating mathematical models of waveguide refractive index shifts under thermal loads, to running finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) electromagnetic simulations across 18 distinct grating coupler geometries, fabricating experimental multi-project wafer lots qualifying as pilot models under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4), and executing bit-error-rate (BER) and eye-diagram laboratory validation tests leading to iterative mask redesigns.
Step 4: Contemporaneous Project Tracking and Substantiation Controls

To satisfy strict judicial substantiation standards—as enforced in Quebe v. United States, Shami v. Commissioner, and Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner—and ensure summary judgment immunity under Tax Court Rule 121, OptiCore must deploy project-level time and supply accounting. The company must implement an automated engineering time-tracking system linked to Jira and EDA project tickets, requiring W-2 engineers to allocate hours daily between qualified R&D activities (such as RTL coding, FDTD simulation, and wafer die testing) and non-qualified activities (such as general administration, customer marketing, and post-production quality control) in accordance with Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(1). All consumed prototype silicon wafers and optical sub-assemblies must be tracked by project work order to substantiate supply QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C). Finally, OptiCore must require SiliconWave to segregate foundry invoices between experimental MPW prototype fabrication runs (eligible for 65 percent contract research treatment under § 41(b)(3)) and commercial volume production runs after design freeze (ineligible post-development manufacturing under § 41(d)(4)(A)).

body.text: 5. Synthesis and Strategic Conclusions for U.S. Tax Practitioners

The Seventh Circuit's ruling in Spellman v. Commissioner remains a cornerstone of United States R&D tax jurisprudence because it pierces the formalistic veneer of research contracts to evaluate their underlying microeconomic incentives. While the U.S. Supreme Court in Snow v. Commissioner ensured that early-stage enterprises are not penalized for incurring research expenditures prior to generating product sales, Spellman established the definitive boundary between a genuine pre-operational business and a passive capital investment.

Three overarching legal principles govern modern compliance planning under Spellman. First, economic reality governs contractual options and residual rights. Tax authorities and federal courts will not respect paper reservations of intellectual property—such as rights to research "byproducts" or contingent commercialization clauses—if an accompanying call option, exclusive license, or capital constraint makes it economically improbable that the taxpayer will ever actively manufacture or market the resulting product. Whenever a counterparty can acquire successful research deliverables for a pre-set price below fair market value, the funding entity's upside is capped like a debt or preferred-equity instrument, destroying the "realistic prospect" of trade or business entry under IRC § 174(a)(1) and automatically disqualifying any associated R&D tax credits under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A).

Second, taxpayers must maintain strict alignment between operational capability, technical governance, and substantial rights. To sustain deductions or amortization under IRC § 174 and tax credits under IRC § 41, a taxpayer outsourcing research must prove both that it retains substantial rights to exploit the research results without paying additional consideration under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3) and that it possesses the internal technical governance, working capital, and operational capability to commercialize those results in its own trade or business.

Third, contemporaneous admissible evidence serves as the sole reliable antidote to summary judgment. Because Spellman empowers the Tax Court under Rule 121 and federal district courts under Rule 56 to dispose of R&D tax claims on summary judgment even when questions of business intent or motive are raised, taxpayers cannot wait until litigation to construct after-the-fact affidavits. Sustaining an R&D claim requires embedding legal and technical substantiation—arm's-length contract risk allocation, Joint Steering Committee oversight, hypothesis-driven laboratory documentation, and granular project cost accounting—directly into the lifecycle of the research program from inception.
